{{Short description|Concept in integral mathematics}}
In [[complex analysis]], the '''estimation lemma''', also known as the '''{{mvar|ML}} inequality'''  (ML for Max times Length), gives an [[upper bound]] for a [[contour integral]]. If {{mvar|f}} is a [[complex number|complex]]-valued, [[continuous function]] on the contour {{math|Γ}} and if its [[absolute value#Complex numbers|absolute value]] {{math|{{abs|''f''&thinsp;(''z'')}}}} is bounded by a constant {{mvar|M}} for all {{mvar|z}} on {{math|&Gamma;}}, then

:<math>\left|\int_\Gamma f(z) \, dz\right| \le M\, l(\Gamma), </math>
where {{math|''l''(Γ)}} is the [[arc length]] of {{math|&Gamma;}}. In particular, we may take the [[maxima and minima|maximum]]

:<math>M:= \sup_{z\in\Gamma}|f(z)|</math>

as upper bound. Intuitively, the [[lemma (mathematics)|lemma]] is very simple to understand. If a contour is thought of as many smaller contour segments connected together, then there will be a maximum {{math|{{abs|''f''&thinsp;(''z'')}}}} for each segment. Out of all the maximum {{math|{{abs|''f''&thinsp;(''z'')}}}}s for the segments, there will be an overall largest one. Hence, if the overall largest {{math|{{abs|''f''&thinsp;(''z'')}}}} is summed over the entire path then the integral of {{math|''f''&thinsp;(''z'')}} over the path must be less than or equal to it.

Formally, the inequality can be shown to hold using the definition of contour integral, the [[Integral#Inequalities for integrals|absolute value inequality for integrals]] and the formula for the [[Curve#Lengths of curves|length of a curve]] as follows:

:<math>\left|\int_\Gamma f(z)\, dz \right| 
= \left|\int_\alpha^\beta f(\gamma(t))\gamma'(t)\, dt \right| 
\leq \int_\alpha^\beta \left|f(\gamma(t))\right|\left|\gamma'(t)\right|\, dt 
\leq M \int_\alpha^\beta \left|\gamma'(t)\right|\, dt = M\, l(\Gamma)</math>

The estimation lemma is most commonly used as part of the [[methods of contour integration]] with the intent to show that the integral over part of a contour goes to zero as {{math|{{abs|''z''}}}} goes to infinity. An example of such a case is shown below.

== Example ==
[[Image:Upper halfcircle with i.svg|thumb|200px|The contour {{math|Γ}}.]]
'''Problem.'''
Find an upper bound for

:<math>\left|\int_\Gamma \frac{1}{(z^2+1)^2} \, dz\right|,</math>

where {{math|Γ}} is the upper half-[[circle]] {{math|{{abs|''z''}} {{=}} ''a''}} with [[radius]] {{math|''a'' > 1}} traversed once in the counterclockwise direction.

'''Solution.'''
First observe that the length of the path of integration is half the [[circumference]] of a circle with radius {{mvar|a}}, hence
:<math>l(\Gamma)=\tfrac{1}{2}(2\pi a)=\pi a.</math>
Next we seek an upper bound {{mvar|M}} for the integrand when {{math|{{abs|''z''}} {{=}} ''a''}}. By the [[triangle inequality]] we see that
:<math>|z|^2=\left|z^2\right| = \left|z^2+1-1\right| \le \left|z^2+1\right|+1,</math>
therefore
:<math>\left|z^2+1\right|\ge |z|^2 - 1 = a^2 - 1>0</math> 
because {{math|{{abs|''z''}} {{=}} ''a'' > 1}} on {{math|Γ}}. Hence
:<math>\left|\frac{1}{\left(z^2+1\right)^2}\right| \le \frac{1}{\left(a^2-1\right)^2}.</math>
Therefore, we apply the estimation lemma with {{math|''M'' {{=}} {{sfrac|1|(''a''<sup>2</sup> − 1)<sup>2</sup>}}}}. The resulting bound is
:<math>\left|\int_\Gamma \frac{1}{\left(z^2+1\right)^2}\,dz\right| \le \frac{\pi a}{\left(a^2-1\right)^2}. </math>
